title: A design loop around an outside solver is read as an objective trace plus a constraint check
summary: Four figures show an optimiser driving external physics codes as black boxes: ignition delay with a temperature ceiling, rocket-nozzle thrust, and an airfoil lift coefficient. Each is read as a best-so-far trace against solver calls, then checked against the constraint and the design variables that matter.

media.alt: Line chart titled as minimising ignition delay subject to a 2320 K temperature ceiling. The y axis is ignition delay in milliseconds from 0 to 0.5; the x axis is cumulative kinetics evaluations from 0 to 80. Red markers sit at about 0.49 ms for the first three points, drop to about 0.338 ms by the eighth evaluation, and stay flat through 80.

source.caption: Constrained optimization convergence — ignition delay minimized against the temperature ceiling
group: 19_19_refining_fire_convergence: ignition delay in ms against cumulative kinetics evaluations (80 plotted), from about 0.49 to about 0.338 (representative)
18_18_refining_fire_poster: reactor temperature against time for the converged design, a dashed horizontal ceiling at 2320 K and a dotted vertical line at the ignition delay (video poster frame)
20_20_nozzle_thrust_convergence: nozzle thrust against cumulative CFD evaluations, 4.328e6 rising to about 4.367e6 in 35 plotted points
21_21_airfoil_optimization_poster: the converged cambered airfoil shape with lift coefficient 1.244 in its title (video poster frame)
source.note: Figure titles name internal tooling (a project solver suite, a Julia subprocess). This page teaches the generic reading and does not describe those tools. The design variables and operating conditions are not on the figures.

read_the_figure.question: How quickly did the objective improve per call of the external solver, and does the converged design respect the constraint it was given?
read_the_figure.axes: Convergence figures: x is cumulative solver calls (each one a real external-process run); y is the objective in physical units (ignition delay in ms; thrust in N-equivalent, with the axis offset by 1e6). Temperature figure: x is time in ms, y is reactor temperature in K, with the ceiling and the ignition time marked. Airfoil: the shape itself, with the lift coefficient in the title.
look_at: A trace that drops steeply and then goes flat has either converged or spent its remaining calls on something other than the plotted objective, such as meeting the constraint.
In the ignition figure, the drop happens by the 8th call and the remaining 70 or so calls leave the value unchanged: the later calls are doing constraint work.
In the nozzle figure, check the y axis labels. The axis starts near 4.328e6 and ends near 4.367e6, so a visually steep rise is a change of under one percent.
In the temperature figure, the final temperature is close to the ceiling line: a binding constraint presses on the optimum, and a slack one would leave a gap.
In the airfoil shape, a strong curved camber line is what a lift-maximising design looks like when lift grows with camber.
read_the_figure.proves: That the loop ran, improved its objective, and ended at a feasible design for one problem. It does not show that the design is globally optimal or that the external model is accurate for the real device.
if_wrong: A trace that keeps improving until the end: the budget is too small, and the final value is not converged.
A final temperature above the ceiling: the design is infeasible and the objective gain is not valid.
An improvement that is small compared with the model's own error is not a design result.
must_check: The constraint is drawn on the figure with its value, as in the temperature figure.
The y axis of any trace states offsets and ranges; a zoomed axis exaggerates small gains.
Which evaluations are plotted: here the markers are sparse and start at the third call, so they are a subset of the evaluations.
The design variables and their bounds, which are not on these figures.
The model's own uncertainty, since a gain smaller than it is not evidence.
as_drawn: Ignition figure: delay about 0.49 ms for the first three plotted calls, then about 0.338 ms from the 8th call onward (read by eye, about 5 percent). That is a reduction of about 31 percent (computed, (0.49 - 0.338) / 0.49). The project text reports 82 calls; the plot ends at 80.

Temperature figure: the curve starts near 1,435 K and rises to near 2,300 K at about 0.337 ms, ending just under the 2,320 K ceiling. The project text gives the converged final temperature as 2,295.4 K, which is 24.6 K under the ceiling (2320 - 2295.4).

Nozzle figure: thrust rises from about 4.328e6 to about 4.367e6, most of it by the 9th call, then creeps up by roughly 0.001e6 over the next 26 calls. The total gain is 0.9 percent (computed: 0.039 / 4.328). The title is cut off at the right edge of the image, and the project text reports 37 calls against 35 on the axis.

Airfoil figure: the shape is a cambered section with its maximum height in the rear half and a lift coefficient of 1.244 in the title. The figure does not give the angle of attack or the camber bounds.

terms.meaning: A function the optimiser can only evaluate by calling an outside program. Its internals and derivatives are not available.
The time for a reacting mixture to reach thermal runaway, often taken as the time of the steepest temperature rise.
A requirement that a quantity stay on one side of a limit, here a peak temperature at or below a ceiling.
A constraint that is active at the optimum: relaxing it would let the objective improve.
Turning a constrained problem into an unconstrained one by adding a cost for violation, with a weight that is increased in steps (continuation).
A derivative-free simplex search, suitable when each evaluation is an external run.
Compressible inviscid flow along a duct whose area varies, a standard reduced model for nozzles.
A linear model in which lift depends on the angle of attack and the camber line, with a lift slope of 2 pi per radian.
The mean curve midway between the upper and lower surface of an airfoil.

remember: Best-so-far against solver calls is the honest cost axis for expensive black-box runs.
Look for the constraint on the figure: without it, an improvement may be infeasible.
A zoomed y axis makes a small change look steep: read the tick labels.
A flat tail after the first drop can hide a lot of work spent on constraint satisfaction.
Optimum under a model is optimum for the model.

understand.title: Why a penalty with continuation
understand.text: A fixed small penalty lets the optimiser cross the limit; a very large one makes the objective ragged and hard to search. Starting small and raising the weight lets the search first find the good region and then be pushed back to the boundary.

understand.title: Why the constraint is binding here
understand.text: Faster ignition comes from a hotter, more reactive state, which also gives a higher peak temperature. The two goals pull the same way, so the best design sits against the temperature ceiling rather than inside it, which is what the small gap to the dashed line shows.

steps.title: The constrained problem
steps.note: The design variables x are not shown on the figure. The objective and constraint are both computed by one external kinetics run.

steps.title: A quadratic penalty
steps.note: Where the constraint holds the penalty term is zero; where it is violated it grows with the square of the excess. Continuation repeats the search with increasing mu.

steps.title: Margin to the ceiling
steps.note: A margin of a few tens of kelvin out of a rise of about 900 K is a binding constraint to within the search's tolerance. The converged value is the project text's, not read from the plot.

steps.title: Relative gain from a trace
steps.note: Reporting the fractional change removes the effect of a zoomed axis: 31 percent for the ignition delay, under one percent for thrust.

steps.title: Lift from the camber line (thin-airfoil theory)
steps.note: More camber lowers the zero-lift angle and raises lift at a given angle of attack. Without bounds on the camber, a lift-maximising loop would push it indefinitely, so the design space or the constraints must limit it. This is the standard textbook relation, which the project's panel code is presumed to follow; the figure does not state it.

worked.title: Gain, margin and axis exaggeration
worked.problem: For the nozzle trace the axis runs from about 4.328e6 to 4.367e6. What fraction of the axis height does the total gain fill, and what is the gain relative to the starting value?

solution.text: The trace spans the axis, so it fills nearly all of it.

worked.answer: The curve fills the plot, but the actual gain is 0.9 percent. The axis choice makes a small improvement look dramatic, which is acceptable for a convergence plot only if the axis label is read.

analyze.q: The ignition trace is flat from the 8th to the 80th call. List two things the later calls could have been doing, and say what extra plot would tell them apart.
analyze.hint: Constraint tightening, step-size shrinking; plot the constraint value against call number.

analyze.q: A 0.9 percent thrust gain from 35 solver calls: under what circumstances is that a meaningful design result?
analyze.hint: Compare with model error and with the effect of manufacturing tolerance.

analyze.q: The airfoil title shows a lift coefficient but not the angle of attack. Why is that a problem for reading the result?
analyze.hint: Lift depends on both camber and angle.

evaluate.q: Do these figures show that the optimiser works, that the model is right, or both? State what each one needs.
Which single piece of extra information would most improve the nozzle convergence figure?
evaluate.hint: Design variables and bounds, or a baseline design for context.

create: Redraw the ignition-delay figure with two stacked panels sharing the call axis: the objective above, and the constraint margin (ceiling minus temperature) below.
Design an airfoil figure that shows the starting shape and the converged shape on the same axes with the angle of attack and the lift coefficients in the legend.

checks.answer: A constraint that the optimum sits on: relaxing it would let the objective improve. In the ignition problem, the temperature ceiling is the one limiting how fast the mixture can ignite.

checks.q: Ignition delay falls from 0.49 ms to 0.338 ms. What percentage reduction is that?
Why may a very steep thrust curve represent a small gain?
checks.answer: Because the y axis spans only about 0.04e6 around 4.33e6. The curve fills the plot, but the total change is under one percent.

checks.q: What does a converged optimum of an external solver tell you about the real device?
checks.answer: Only that the design is best for that model and those conditions. It says nothing about the real device unless the model has been validated for that regime.

checks.q: How would you show that the penalty continuation worked?
checks.hint: Plot the constraint violation against call number.
checks.answer: Plot the constraint violation, the maximum of zero and temperature minus ceiling, against the call number with the penalty weight steps marked. It should fall to zero as the weight rises.
